Empirical Research Plan:  Compulsory Schooling, Educational Attainment, and Earnings

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Instrumental‐Variables (2SLS).  
Quarter-of-birth (QOB) supplies exogenous variation in years of schooling because U.S. states fix (i) the school-entry cut-off date and (ii) the minimum school-leaving age in years, not grades. Children born just after the cut-off are forced to start school a year later and therefore must remain enrolled one grade longer before they legally may drop out. QOB therefore shifts completed schooling but is plausibly unrelated to potential earnings except through schooling. Given the discrete nature of QOB—and the fact that the “first-stage” jump in schooling is incomplete—this is a classic fuzzy instrument rather than a sharp regression discontinuity.

Why not DID or RDD?  
• We have no policy change over time (so DID is inapplicable).  
• Exact birth-date running variable would be ideal for RDD, but we only observe QOB; the 3-month bin makes the running variable too coarse for local comparison.  
Hence IV is the cleanest, widely accepted design for this setting.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable (endogenous): S_i  = completed years of schooling for individual i.  

Instrument (Z_i): First-quarter birth indicator  
 Z_i = 1 if born in Jan–Mar, 0 if born in Oct–Dec. (Robustness: use full set of QOB dummies or a linear function 1–4.)

Control group: Individuals born in the fourth quarter (Oct–Dec).  
(We exclude second and third quarters in the baseline to maximize first‐stage contrast; they return in robustness checks.)

Treatment timing: Education earned before age 25; outcomes (earnings) measured at Census enumeration (ages 25–55).

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Relevance: QOB must predict schooling.  
 Plausible—well-documented 0.10–0.20 year gap between Q1 and Q4 births.

A2. Independence / Random Assignment: Conditional on state- and year-of-birth fixed effects, QOB is as-good-as-random.  
 Plausible—seasonality in births exists but is small once we control for mother’s age, race, and region.

A3. Exclusion Restriction: QOB affects adult earnings only through its impact on schooling.  
 Plausible though not guaranteed—season-of-birth could affect health; will be probed via placebo tests (height, disability).

A4. Monotonicity: Being born in Q1 weakly reduces schooling relative to Q4 for everyone (no “defiers”).  
 Plausible given compulsory attendance laws; parents rarely lobby to reverse entry timing.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment (SUTVA): One child’s QOB does not affect another child’s outcomes.  
 Highly plausible.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Seasonality in Family Background  
 • Control for sex, race, mother’s age, state-by-year fixed effects.  
 • Show balance on predetermined covariates by QOB.  
 • Estimate reduced-form effect of QOB on covariates (should be ≈0).

T2. Weak Instrument Concern (relevance < 10 F-stat)  
 • Report first-stage F-statistic; if < 10, use LIML and Anderson-Rubin CIs.  
 • Pool adjacent cohorts to strengthen first stage if needed.

T3. Direct Biological/Health Channel (exclusion)  
 • Add controls for early-life mortality proxy (infant-mortality rate in birth state-year).  
 • Placebo on outcomes unlikely affected by schooling (height, number of children) to detect direct effects.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)    # fast 2SLS (feols)
library(AER)       # ivreg as fallback
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------------
census <- fread("census_qob_1930_1959.csv")   # user-supplied path

# 2. Variable construction -------------------------------------------------
census[, qob := quarter(birth_date)]          # 1–4
census[, firstq := as.integer(qob == 1)]
census[, fourthq := as.integer(qob == 4)]

# Outcome & controls
census[, l_earn := log(wage_income)]          # winsorize outside code
census[, age := census_year - birth_year]
census[, age_sq := age^2]

# 3. Baseline 2SLS ---------------------------------------------------------
# Keep Q1 and Q4 only
sample <- census[qob %in% c(1,4) & age %between% c(25,55)]

iv_baseline <- feols(
  l_earn ~ 1 | 
    . ~ firstq,                                   # first stage
  iv = ~ educ | firstq,                           # 2SLS syntax
  data = sample,
  cluster = ~ state_birth*birth_year              # clustered SEs
)

summary(iv_baseline, se = "cluster")

# 4. Reduced form & first stage checks -------------------------------------
rf <- feols(l_earn ~ firstq + age + age_sq | state_birth + birth_year,
            data = sample, cluster = ~ state_birth*birth_year)

fs <- feols(educ ~ firstq + age + age_sq | state_birth + birth_year,
            data = sample, cluster = ~ state_birth*birth_year)

wald_iv <- coef(rf)["firstq"] / coef(fs)["firstq"]

# 5. Robustness: four-quarter instrument -----------------------------------
iv_4q <- feols(
  l_earn ~ 1 | 
    . ~ factor(qob),                 # full set of QOB dummies
  iv = ~ educ | factor(qob),
  data = census[age %between% c(25,55)],
  cluster = ~ state_birth*birth_year
)

# Weak-instrument robust inference
library(ivreg)
iv_liml <- ivreg(l_earn ~ educ + age + age_sq | factor(qob) + age + age_sq,
                 data = census)
coeftest(iv_liml, vcov = vcovCL, cluster = ~ state_birth*birth_year)
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Economic theory and prior literature suggest each additional year of schooling raises log earnings by 8 – 12 percent. The IV estimate should be at the upper end (≈ 10 percent) because it captures the return to marginal students compelled to stay in school longer—likely those with higher returns to education than the average.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Relevance (F > 10) ............................................ 1  
C2: Independence (no covariate imbalance) ......................... 0.8  
C3: Exclusion (no direct QOB→earnings path) ....................... 0.6  
C4: Monotonicity (no “defiers”) ................................... 1  
C5: Correct functional form / no heterogeneous treatment bias ..... 0.8  

Total (out of 5) = 4.2 ➜ Reasonably strong but not bullet-proof.

────────────────────────────────────────
End of Plan
